opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one we think about a lot. The honest answer is that a lot of the ingredients are already there. Diffusion models for language use the same backbone as autoregressive models. It's still a transformer; the main difference is the training objective and how you generate at inference time. So much of the infrastructure the community has built over the past several years, the parallelism strategies, the hardware optimizations, the data pipelines, carries over pretty directly. You're not starting from scratch.

What we've seen empirically is that diffusion language models seem to follow scaling laws similar to autoregressive models. As you add compute, data, and parameters, the loss goes down in a predictable way. There may be a constant-factor difference in efficiency, depending on how you set things up, but the qualitative behavior is encouraging. It suggests there's no fundamental wall you hit at larger scales.

Where it gets interesting is that the trade-offs are different. With autoregressive models, you get one token per forward pass, so inference cost scales with sequence length in a very rigid way. With diffusion, you're refining the whole sequence in parallel over a number of denoising steps, and you can trade off quality against speed by choosing how many steps to take. As models get bigger, that matters more, because inference cost becomes the dominant concern for deployment. Being able to generate many tokens at once and use the GPU much more efficiently is a big part of why we think this is the right direction to scale.

There are open research questions, of course. How do you best adapt things like post-training, RLHF, and instruction tuning to a diffusion setting? A lot of those techniques were designed with left-to-right generation in mind, so you have to rethink them a bit. There are also questions about the right noise process for discrete data, how to handle variable-length outputs, and how to get the most out of reasoning-style workloads. But I see those as engineering and research problems we're making steady progress on, not fundamental blockers.

So my view is that the path is pretty clear: take what works in the autoregressive world, adapt the parts that are specific to the generation process, and push on compute. Every time we've scaled up so far, the models have gotten better in the ways we'd hope, and the speed advantages stay. That's what makes me optimistic.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question we get a lot, because for a long time the conventional wisdom was that diffusion works beautifully for images and video but just doesn't scale for text. And I think what we've shown with Mercury, and what others have shown in parallel, is that that's not really true. The scaling behavior is actually quite similar to autoregressive models. If you plot loss or downstream performance against compute, you see curves that look very familiar. So the first thing I'd say is there's no fundamental wall that we've hit.

The way I think about it is that there are really two axes. One is just the standard scaling recipe: more parameters, more data, more compute, and getting the engineering right so you can train efficiently at that scale. A lot of that transfers directly from what the autoregressive world has figured out over the past several years. Architecturally, these models are still transformers. We can reuse most of the infrastructure, the data pipelines, the optimization tricks. So in that sense, it's a known path.

The second axis is more specific to diffusion, and this is where I think the interesting research is. With an autoregressive model, you're committed to a particular factorization of the joint distribution. Left to right, one token at a time. Diffusion gives you a lot more freedom in how you generate: how many tokens you commit to at each step, in what order, how many denoising steps you take. And that's a design space that hasn't been explored nearly as thoroughly. So part of scaling is figuring out how the optimal inference procedure changes as the model gets bigger. Our intuition, and we're seeing some evidence of this, is that larger models are actually better at parallel generation. They can predict more tokens correctly at once, which means you need fewer steps, which means the speed advantage actually gets larger with scale rather than smaller.

There's also the question of how you leverage existing pretrained models. One thing that's become clear is you don't necessarily have to start from scratch. You can take an autoregressive model and adapt it into a diffusion model with a relatively modest amount of additional compute, and that gives you a very practical on-ramp to large scale without having to redo all of the pretraining.

And then the last thing I'd say is that the economics matter a lot here. The reason we care about scaling diffusion language models isn't just academic. If you can get frontier-level quality at five or ten times the throughput, that changes what applications are feasible. Agents, code generation, anything where you're generating a lot of tokens and latency is the bottleneck. So the path to scale is partly technical, but it's also about demonstrating that at each size, the model is competitive on quality while keeping that speed advantage. That's what we've been focused on, and so far the trend is encouraging.

astra-6.text:
I think the big question is whether the advantages of diffusion can translate into better quality for a given amount of compute. You can make the model larger, but you also have to think about the training objective, the data, and how you’re going to generate text at inference time.

One appealing property is that you can generate or refine multiple tokens in parallel. But that doesn’t automatically make generation cheaper, because you’re doing multiple rounds of refinement. So there’s a tradeoff: how many steps do you need, and how much useful work can you do in each step?

I would think about scaling as a joint problem of model size and algorithm design. We need to understand how performance improves with more training compute, and then compare models under realistic inference budgets. That would tell us whether we’re getting a compelling alternative to autoregressive models, and where the advantages are strongest.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of room to scale, but it’s not just a question of making the model bigger. You also have to figure out the right training recipe and how to use computation effectively at inference time.

With an autoregressive model, you generate one token at a time. With diffusion, you can update many tokens in parallel, but you typically do multiple rounds of refinement. So there’s a tradeoff: how much work do you do in each round, and how many rounds do you need? That’s something we need to optimize together with the architecture and the training objective.

The encouraging thing is that we can borrow a lot from the infrastructure developed for large language models. We don’t have to reinvent everything. But I wouldn’t assume that the best choices for autoregressive models are also the best choices for diffusion. We need experiments at larger scales to understand that.

And I think the interesting question is not only whether we can match autoregressive models on standard benchmarks, but whether we can take advantage of this different way of generating text—for example, being able to revise a whole sequence or generate under constraints. That could make scaling worthwhile beyond simply reproducing what existing models already do.
